facts.fact: ArcFace (Deng, Guo, Yang, Xue, Kotsia, Zafeiriou) was published at CVPR 2019 and proposes an additive angular margin loss; the name comes from the fact that the additive angular margin equals the geodesic distance margin on the normalised hypersphere.
The ArcFace paper reports state-of-the-art results on ten face recognition benchmarks; the arXiv abstract also describes a sub-center variant for noisy data.

MICA (Zielonka, Bolkart, Thies, ECCV 2022, arXiv 2204.06607) uses a pretrained ArcFace network as its identity encoder, followed by a small mapping network into the latent space of a geometry decoder.
In MICA, most of the ArcFace network is frozen and only the last 3 ResNet blocks are fine-tuned; the authors state that refining more hidden layers led to worse predictions due to overfitting.

MICA's training objective, per the search snippet of its Eq. 1, is a masked supervised 3D geometry loss against ground-truth 3D shapes; no separate ArcFace feature or identity-matching term was found in the snippets. This contradicts the premise that MICA uses an ArcFace identity loss.
MICA reports 15% and 24% lower average reconstruction error than state-of-the-art methods on the NoW benchmark (non-metric and metric variants respectively), as stated in its abstract.
MICA's authors argue that ArcFace features are robust to expression, illumination and camera changes, so supervised shape learning on top of them generalises well.

FaceNet (arXiv 1503.03832) performs verification by thresholding the squared L2 distance between embeddings and reports 99.63% LFW accuracy; this figure came from a search-result summary and was not checked against the paper text.
LFW results are usually reported under a 10-fold protocol in which the threshold is tuned on nine folds and applied to the held-out fold, with accuracies averaged.
For unit-normalised embeddings, cosine similarity and L2 distance are monotonically related, so a threshold must be converted between the two when switching metrics.

Thresholds are model- and dataset-specific; a threshold chosen on one dataset may not transfer. Practitioners recommend sweeping the threshold on one's own labelled pairs to hit a target false-accept rate. No canonical cosine threshold for ArcFace-style models was found.
One LFW-based study cites a conventional fixed cosine threshold of 0.5 and reports that its adaptive threshold performed better; this is a single secondary-source claim, not verified.
The InsightFace model zoo lists the buffalo_l pack as SCRFD-10GF detection plus ResNet50 trained on WebFace600K recognition, about 326 MB in total.

The buffalo_l recognition file w600k_r50.onnx is about 166 MB and outputs 512-dimensional embeddings; SCRFD (det_10g.onnx) is needed for detection. These figures come from third-party project READMEs and were not verified against the official zoo.

Third-party projects state the InsightFace pretrained models are licensed for non-commercial research only, separately from the MIT-licensed code. This is a secondary claim and must be verified against the official license before commercial use.

Mirror downloads of buffalo_l (SourceForge, Hugging Face, and GitHub release assets) are community-hosted, not official; one README claims they match the official file, which is unverified. SHA-256 verification is advisable.
The official InsightFace CLI for the older 0.3.2 package downloads the pack with `insightface-cli model.download buffalo_l`; the local default path is typically ~/.insightface/models/buffalo_l/.

contradictions: The task premise says MICA uses ArcFace as an identity loss; the MICA search result says ArcFace is a frozen identity encoder and the training loss is a supervised 3D geometry loss.

Thresholds: FaceNet uses squared L2 distance on its own scale; a third-party LFW study cites a cosine 0.5 threshold; another system used 0.08-0.09. These are not comparable without the model and metric.
